messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The war had been over for more than fifty years, but for Phong, it had never truly ended. He was a boy of sixteen when soldiers came to his village in the Mekong Delta. He remembered the smell of smoke and wet earth, the shouting, and then the hands—rough hands that grabbed him by the collar and forced him to the ground. They tied his wrists behind his back with a length of nylon rope, so tight that the fibers bit into his skin. He lay there for hours, face pressed into the mud, listening to the crackle of burning bamboo and the voices of men who spoke a language he could not understand. That night was etched into him with a clarity that had not faded with the decades. The memory returned not as a story he told himself, but as a sudden, overwhelming descent—a vivid, full-color re-experiencing that left him breathless and disoriented. Something in his surroundings could bring it all back without any warning at all.

Now, at seventy-six, Phong worked the night shift at a distribution warehouse in Sacramento. The work was solitary and physically demanding, which suited him. He stacked boxes onto pallets in a quiet corner of the building, far from the supervisors and the other men. But the warehouse was not safe. The smell of cardboard and dust, the hum of the fluorescent lights—these were neutral enough. It was the unexpected moments that undid him. A new worker once clapped him on the shoulder from behind, and Phong’s body locked rigid. He felt the rope again, the pressure on his wrists, the helplessness. The smell of the man’s cheap cologne, sharp and synthetic, seemed to hang in the air long after he had walked away. That smell became a trigger. He started avoiding the break room, where the air was thick with deodorant and sweat. Then there were the confrontations. A younger worker, impatient with Phong’s slow pace, raised his voice one evening. Phong did not shout back. He simply stopped moving. His hands trembled. The shouting was not loud by any standard, but it was enough to send him back to that night—to the soldiers’ voices, to the feeling of being pinned down with no way out. The memory itself, once triggered, made him hyper-vigilant. He began scanning the aisles before he walked down them. He positioned his pallet jack so that his back was always to a wall. He came to believe that if he could just control his environment, he could keep the memories at bay.

But the memories did not stay at bay. They returned without warning, and when they did, they overwhelmed him completely. He would have to stop what he was doing, gripping the metal shelf until his knuckles went white, waiting for the feeling to pass. The emotion was not just fear—it was a crushing sense of helplessness, the same helplessness he had felt as a boy on the ground. The vividness of the memory, the clarity of the smells and the sounds and the pressure, made it feel as though no time had passed at all. And each time the memory came, it seemed to sharpen his sensitivity to the triggers in his environment. A faint smell of rain on asphalt could now make him pause. The sight of a coiled hose in the warehouse aisle made him take a different route. He was certain that if he let his guard down, the memory would catch him again.

The cycle had worn him down. He had stopped visiting the corner market where the cashier, a friendly woman, wore a perfume that reminded him of something he could not name. He had not spoken to his neighbor in months, because the man sometimes argued with his wife, and the sound of raised voices made Phong’s chest tighten. His supervisor had noticed his isolation, his refusal to work near others. There had been a warning. Phong knew he was at risk of losing the job. It was this, finally, that brought him to the clinic. He sat in the waiting room with his hands folded in his lap, staring at the floor. What frightened him most was not the memory itself, but the certainty that he could not stop it from coming back. He hoped, quietly, that someone might tell him how to make it stop.
